title: Suprachoroidal Vitreopexy & Buckling: Minimal Invasive Retinal Surgery
summary: Suprachoroidal vitreopexy (suprachoroidal buckling) is a state-of-the-art, minimally invasive technique that utilizes the suprachoroidal space (SCS) to create a localized internal chorioretinal indentation. By injecting hydrogels, viscoelastics, or long-acting agents into the SCS, surgeons can seal retinal breaks in rhegmatogenous retinal detachment without conjunctival peritomy, extraocular muscle manipulation, or scleral sutures.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Suprachoroidal vitreopexy (or suprachoroidal buckling - SCB) is a sutureless, extraocular vitreoretinal procedure designed to repair primary rhegmatogenous retinal detachments (RRD). By cannulating the potential space between the sclera and choroid (the suprachoroidal space), biocompatible viscoelastic agents, long-acting cross-linked hydrogels, or autologous products are injected to create a precise inward choroidal bulge. This localized buckle closes the retinal break, alleviates vitreoretinal traction, and facilitates subretinal fluid reabsorption without requiring extensive conjunctival dissection, scleral suturing, or intraocular vitrectomy.

branches: Vitreoretinal Traction Relief: Inward displacement of choroid neutralizes anteroposterior vitreous pull
Break Opposition: Approximates RPE monolayer to neurosensory retinal edges
Fluid Pump Activation: Restoration of RPE active transport pumps to clear subretinal fluid
Adhesion Enhancement: Synergizes with pre- or intraoperative cryopexy/laser photocoagulation

rows: Reversible, smooth dome indentation, optimal seal time
Transient duration; risk of early redetachment
Variable degradation rate, potential vitreous haze

sections.title: Patient Selection & Clinical Indications
content: Primary Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RRD) with single or closely clustered peripheral retinal tears.
Retinal breaks located in the superior, nasal, or temporal quadrants (equatorial to anterior location).
Absence of severe Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR limited to Grade A or B).
Phakic or pseudophakic eyes with clear optical media allowing accurate indirect ophthalmoscopic visualization.
Patients unfit for or seeking to avoid refractive shifts associated with traditional scleral buckling or gas tamponade posture.

sections.title: Preoperative Diagnostic Workup
content: Widefield Fundus Imaging (Optos): Precise mapping of break position, clock hours, and retinal detachment extent.
360-Degree Scleral Depression Exam: Detection of secondary atrophic holes, lattice degeneration, or vitreoretinal tufts.
Enhanced Depth Imaging OCT (EDI-OCT): High-resolution baseline assessment of choroidal thickness and macula status.
B-Scan Ultrasonography (10-20 MHz): Measurement of subretinal fluid height and exclusion of posterior choroidal detachments.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Surgical Technique Protocol
content: Step 1: Localized Retinopexy: Apply transpupillary 532nm/810nm laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy around the targeted retinal break.
Step 2: Micro-Scleral Access: Perform a minimal radial scleral incision (1-2mm) or insert a custom 27G/30G micro-cannula 4-6mm posterior to the limbus.
Step 3: Suprachoroidal Cannulation: Advance the flexible blunt cannula into the suprachoroidal space toward the meridian of the retinal break.
Step 4: Controlled Injection: Slowly inject cross-linked HA or hydrogel gel (0.2 - 0.5 mL) under direct indirect ophthalmoscopy (BIO) guidance.
Step 5: Indentation Verification: Confirm elevation of the choroidal mound directly underneath and supporting the retinal tear.
Step 6: IOP & Perfusion Monitoring: Measure intraocular pressure; perform anterior chamber paracentesis if IOP exceeds 30 mmHg to maintain central retinal artery perfusion.

sections.title: Intraoperative & Postoperative Complications
content: Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage: Caused by accidental rupture of long posterior ciliary arteries/veins during cannulation.
Subretinal Infiltration of Filler: Migration of hydrogel into subretinal space via an undetected or large break.
Acute IOP Elevation: Transient ocular hypertension secondary to rapid volumetric expansion within the scleral cavity.
Under-Indentation or Early Absorption: Premature loss of buckle height prior to solid chorioretinal scar formation (<14 days).
Transient Choroidal Detachment: Serous effusion surrounding the localized suprachoroidal injection mound.

sections.title: Red Flags & Emergency Escalation Signs
content: Sudden loss of Light Perception (LP) or CRAO signs: Immediate anterior chamber paracentesis required for severe IOP spike.
Dark, expanding suprachoroidal mass accompanied by severe deep ocular pain indicating massive Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage.
Fish-mouth phenomenon or new macula-threatening fluid progression post-injection.
Signs of acute intraocular infection, severe anterior chamber fibrin, or endophthalmitis within 24–72 hours.

sections.title: High-Yield Exam & Surgical Pearls
content: Prophylactic Paracentesis: Always prepare an anterior chamber paracentesis set-up when plan includes injecting >0.25 mL into the SCS.
Optimal Scar Timing: Retinopexy chorioretinal adhesion takes 10-14 days for maximal tensile strength; ensure hydrogel stability >3 weeks.
EDI-OCT Monitoring: EDI-OCT is the ideal modality postoperatively to confirm choroidal mound height and rule out subretinal fluid accumulation.
Avoid Over-Indentation: Ischemic choroidal pallor lasting >15 minutes indicates excessive focal pressure; titrate volume carefully.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Evidence
content: Microneedle Delivery Systems: Development of custom 900–1100 µm microneedles enabling precise suprachoroidal access without scleral cutdown.
Thermo-Responsive Hydrogels: In-situ forming polymers that inject as low-viscosity liquid at room temperature and transition to a firm gel at body temperature (37°C).

Co-Delivery Platform (Combination Therapy): Simultaneous delivery of anti-VEGF agents or steroids (e.g., suprachoroidal triamcinolone acetonide) with indenting polymers to prevent PVR and macular edema.
Clinical Trial Data: Multicenter studies show non-inferior primary anatomical success compared to conventional scleral buckling (88-92%), with superior patient comfort scores and zero myopic shift.

sections.title: Special Population Considerations
content: High Myopia (> -6.00 D): Thin sclera increases risk of scleral perforation into vitreous; microneedle depth calibration is critical.
Pediatric Detachments: Increased scleral elasticity in young patients can cause faster dissipation of suprachoroidal pressure; long-acting cross-linked gels are preferred.
Aphakic / Pseudophakic Eyes: Increased risk of anterior fluid shift; close monitoring of anterior chamber angle configuration is required post-injection.
